---
title: "Biological Reference Points"
---

## Overview

::: {.background-callout}
Biological reference points (BRPs) are a fundamental aspect of fisheries management that determine when a stock is overfished or experiencing overfishing, and inform rebuilding plans and catch advice. BRPs typically assume that growth, natural mortality, maturity, and recruitment are constant over time. However, climate change can influence stock productivity and violate the assumptions in stock assessment and estimation of BRPs. If BRPs are not updated to reflect changing productivity, management may lead to overly optimistic catch advice, delayed rebuilding timelines, or target stock levels that are no longer attainable The redefinition of reference points to reflect current stock productivity is one of the key management challenges in the Northeast U.S. and this challenge will become more pervasive as climate change accelerates. 
Recent examples of redefining BRPs in New England include incorporating updated recruitment stanzas, environmental covariates, and time-varying productivity. Additional methods have been applied globally. There are challenges with each method and how to address non-stationarity in stock productivity in the context of reference points remains an open question. This work will inform best practices in estimating reference points  in our changing ecosystem.

:::

::: callout-note
### Key Objective

Advance approaches in accounting for climate change in defining biological reference points.
:::

### Current Initiatives

::: {.background-callout}
-   **Stakeholder Engagement:** Engage scientists and fisheries stakeholders in the region with the aim of co-developing best practices and providing guidance on the topic
-   **Synthesis Work:** Conduct synthesis to characterize approaches to defining reference points in the US and responsive approaches to ecosystem change in the US and globally
-   **Simulation Testing:** Conduct simulation testing to assess the performance of status quo and alternative approaches to defining reference points in a changing Northeast US shelf ecosystem
-   **Retrospective Analysis:** Apply retrospective analysis to assess changes in reference points over time compared to dynamic reference points
:::
